title: Shine like stars (Philippians 2:12–18)
hookLine: do everything without grumbling, shining like stars
last: ALL THE WAY DOWN, FOR OTHERS.

lines: COUNT YOUR COMPLAINTS FOR A MORNING.
THE BACKGROUND NOISE OF BEING HUMAN.
cards: Count your complaints for one morning. Not the big ones. The coffee's cold.
The traffic. The meeting that could've been an email. The weather, which you can't change and mention anyway.
It's easy to lose count before lunch. Grumbling is a kind of background noise of being human.
So it's a little startling that, right after the hymn of Christ emptying himself, Paul comes down to earth and says: do everything without grumbling.

teach.h: WORK IT OUT, FOR GOD IS AT WORK IN YOU.
teach.b: First, a well-known and much-argued line. In the King James Bible: "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling." And immediately: "For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure."
You work it out, because God is working in you. Christians balance those two halves differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often stress cooperation with grace.

Many Protestants stress that the working out flows from a salvation already given. Read either way, the two sentences belong together. Then the practical part: "Do all things without murmurings and disputings."
Some readers hear an echo of Israel in the wilderness, where the King James uses the same word, murmur, for complaints about the food and the water on the long road out of Egypt.
If the echo is meant, Paul is reaching for a story his own scriptures already told about how hard trust is on a long road.
Then the picture: "That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world."
Crooked and perverse echoes the song of Moses in Deuteronomy.

And the word for lights is phosteres, the word the old Greek translation of Genesis uses for the lights God set in the sky: sun, moon and stars. So a small church in a Roman town can be like stars in a dark sky.
Not by being loud, but by not grumbling, by holding forth the word of life.
And a quiet line about himself: if my life is poured out like an offering, I'm glad.

teach.h: AMONG WHOM YE SHINE AS LIGHTS IN THE WORLD.

how: Some Christians take on a fast from complaining for a day or a season, especially in Lent, and some families and youth groups use Philippians 2:14–15 for it.

games.q: what's inside Philippians 2:12–18 — tap the pairs.
p: how to work out your salvation
lights in the sky, as in Genesis

s: 'work out your own salvation' stands alone in Paul's letter
the next line: "For it is God which worketh in you." the two go together.
'crooked and perverse' echoes the song of Moses
Deuteronomy 32 speaks of a perverse and crooked generation.
the Greek word for 'lights' here is the word for the sun, moon and stars in Genesis
phosteres, in the old Greek translation of Genesis 1.

games.q: you're writing to a small church surrounded by a culture that doesn't share its faith. how do you tell them to stand out?
o: do everything without grumbling, and shine as lights.
games.why: "Do all things without murmurings and disputings... among whom ye shine as lights in the world."

practice: Notice a complaint already forming about today, name it, and let it go on the out-breath; then do the same with the next one.

Picture the moments you're most likely to grumble, the commute, a certain coworker, the dinner dishes, and picture meeting each with quiet instead, or even something kind. If you pray, you can ask for help with the hardest one.

wordCard.voice: Phosteres. Greek for lights, the word Genesis uses for the sun, moon and stars: Paul's picture for a small church, shining without grumbling in a dark sky.

orig.note: Greek: lights, luminaries. used in the Septuagint for the sun, moon and stars of Genesis 1.

carryVoice: Your line: shine as lights. Stars don't shout. That's day six hundred sixty-one.
